title: The Tell-Tale Heart
focus: guilt that the mind cannot hide

teacherSummary.text: An unnamed narrator insists he is sane while describing how the old man's pale blue 'vulture eye' drove him to murder. He spies on the old man for seven nights, kills him on the eighth, dismembers the body and hides it under the floorboards. When police arrive he chats calmly, but a beating sound he believes is the dead man's heart grows louder until he shrieks a confession.

context.history: Poe published the story in 1843. Insanity was a live legal question: the 1843 M'Naghten case in Britain set the test for an insanity defense in the same year. Poe's narrators often argue their own case.

significance: It is one of the most taught examples of an unreliable first-person narrator; every claim of calm reason undercuts itself.
discussionQuestions: The narrator keeps telling us he is not mad. Why might someone insist so hard on a point?
Where does point of view appear in this story, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this story connect to the book's larger concern with guilt and conscience?
